public.prompt: The Head of Operations at QuickShip asked for an analysis to decide whether to add couriers in Lagos. Your analysis surfaces four findings: (1) Lagos average delivery time rose to 30.1 minutes, (2) Kano has notable delivery-time variability, (3) one courier is unusually fast, (4) Abuja is on target. Which finding should open the report, and why?

options.text: Lagos average delivery time rose to 30.1 minutes — it is directly relevant to the staffing decision established in scoping.
Kano's delivery-time variability — it is the most analytically interesting finding in the dataset.
The unusually fast courier — it is a positive finding and stakeholders prefer good news first.
Abuja is on target — it provides useful context before presenting the problem cities.

opt_lagos.message: Correct. The scoping stage established the decision: whether to add Lagos couriers. The Lagos slowdown is the finding most directly relevant to that decision, so it leads.

opt_kano.message: Analytical interestingness is not the right criterion. The scoping stage established the decision as whether to add Lagos couriers — Kano's variability does not inform that decision.

opt_courier.message: Stakeholder preference for good news is not the right criterion. The scoping stage established the decision as whether to add Lagos couriers — the fast courier finding does not inform that decision.

opt_abuja.message: Context about a city that is on target does not help the operations manager decide about Lagos staffing. Lead with the finding that directly informs the decision.

correct.message: Right. The engagement and scoping stage establishes how the analysis will inform decisions. That decision — whether to add Lagos couriers — points to which finding matters most: the Lagos slowdown.

incorrect.message: Think about what the operations manager needs to decide. The scoping stage established the decision; the finding that most directly informs that decision should lead.

hints: What decision did the scoping stage establish for this analysis?
Which finding most directly tells the operations manager whether to add Lagos couriers?

public.prompt: You have three findings to include in the QuickShip operations report: (A) Lagos average delivery time is 30.1 minutes — above the 25-minute target; (B) Kano also misses the target at 26.4 minutes; (C) Abuja is on target at 23.7 minutes. Using the inverted pyramid principle, which ordering is correct?

options.text: A first, then B, then C — most important to least important.
C first, then B, then A — build up to the most important finding.
B first, then A, then C — start with the secondary miss before the primary one, to build context.
A first, then C, then B — lead with the primary finding, then show the on-target city before the secondary miss.

opt_abc.message: Correct. The inverted pyramid puts the most important information first and arranges everything else from most to least important. Lagos (primary finding) leads, then Kano (secondary miss), then Abuja (on target).

opt_cba.message: Building up to the most important finding is a narrative technique, not the inverted pyramid. The inverted pyramid puts the most important information first so the reader gets the key message immediately.

opt_bac.message: Starting with the secondary miss before the primary one does not follow the inverted pyramid. The inverted pyramid ranks by importance to the decision — Lagos is primary because it directly informs the staffing decision, so it must come first.

opt_acb.message: Inserting the on-target city between the two misses breaks the most-to-least-important order. The inverted pyramid keeps findings in descending order of importance.

correct.message: Correct. The inverted pyramid: most important first, then everything else from most to least important.

incorrect.message: The inverted pyramid means the most important information comes first, with everything else arranged from most to least important after that.

hints: The inverted pyramid is about importance, not narrative build-up.
Which city's finding is most important to the Lagos staffing decision?

public.prompt: The Head of Operations asked: should we add couriers in Lagos? Your analysis produced five findings. Drag them into the order they should appear in the stakeholder summary — most relevant to the decision first, least relevant last.

items.text: Lagos average delivery time rose to 30.1 minutes — above the 25-minute target.
Kano also misses the target at 26.4 minutes.
Abuja is on target at 23.7 minutes.
Kano has the most variable delivery times of the three cities.
One Lagos courier completes deliveries 20% faster than the city average.

follow_up.prompt: Which principle best explains why you placed the first finding at the top?

options.text: It is the finding most directly relevant to the staffing decision established in scoping.
It is the most analytically novel finding in the dataset.
It has the largest numerical deviation from the target.

grading.loop_back_note: The Lagos finding must be first (directly informs the staffing decision). The fast-courier finding and Kano variability are analytically interesting but not relevant to the Lagos staffing decision, so they rank last.

correct.message: Well done. You led with the Lagos finding — the one most directly relevant to the staffing decision — and placed analytically interesting but decision-irrelevant findings at the end.

incorrect.message: The inverted pyramid puts the finding most relevant to the stakeholder's decision first. The scoping stage established the decision: whether to add Lagos couriers. Lead with the Lagos finding.

hints: What decision did the scoping stage establish? Which finding most directly informs that decision?
Analytical interestingness (variability, fast courier) is not the right criterion — relevance to the decision is.

public.prompt: Which of the following is a properly framed recommendation — one that makes clear to the audience both what they need to know and what they are being asked to do?

options.text: We recommend adding one Lagos courier; please approve the added headcount.
Lagos delivery times rose to 30 minutes — above the 25-minute target.
Something should be done about Lagos delivery times.
Lagos delivery times are significantly above target and this is a serious problem.

opt_proper.message: Correct. This statement names the action (add one Lagos courier) and includes an explicit ask (please approve the added headcount), making clear what the audience needs to know and what they are being asked to do.

opt_finding_only.message: This is a finding — it describes what the data shows. A recommendation must go further and state what action should be taken and what the reader is being asked to approve.

opt_vague.message: This statement is too vague to be actionable. A recommendation must name the specific action and include an explicit ask — the audience cannot be assumed to know what 'something' means.

opt_restate.message: This restates the finding more emphatically but still does not tell the operations manager what to do. A recommendation must name the action and the explicit ask.

correct.message: Correct. A well-formed recommendation names the action and includes an explicit ask, so the audience knows exactly what decision is in front of them.

incorrect.message: A recommendation must do two things: name the action to take, and include an explicit ask so the audience knows what they are being asked to approve or do.

hints: Does the statement name a specific action, or does it only describe the data?
Does the statement include an explicit ask — something the reader is being asked to approve or do?

public.intro: The Head of Operations needs a recommendation, not just a finding. Use the delivery summary to identify which city's finding should be paired with an actionable recommendation.

tasks.prompt: Select the row for the city whose finding most directly requires an actionable recommendation to the Head of Operations about Lagos courier staffing.
Select the cell that shows the delivery-time value that makes the recommendation necessary — the value that exceeds the target.

task_select_city.correct: Correct. Lagos is the city whose finding directly informs the staffing decision — it is the finding that needs to be paired with an actionable recommendation.
task_select_city.incorrect: The Head of Operations asked about Lagos courier staffing. Which city's finding directly informs that decision?

task_select_value.correct: Correct. The average delivery time of 30.1 minutes exceeds the 25-minute target — this is the finding value that makes the recommendation necessary.
task_select_value.incorrect: Look for the delivery-time value that exceeds the target. That is the finding that the recommendation must address.

correct.message: Correct. You identified the finding (Lagos avg 30.1 min > 25 min target) that needs to be paired with an actionable recommendation. The value of analytical efforts is only realized when insights are acted upon.

incorrect.message: Identify the city whose finding directly informs the staffing decision, then find the delivery-time value that exceeds the target — that is the finding that needs a recommendation.

hints: The Head of Operations asked about Lagos courier staffing — which city's finding is most relevant?
A recommendation is needed when a finding shows a problem that requires action. Which value exceeds the target?

public.prompt: Which of the following best describes the role of the opening section in a findings narrative?

options.text: A short paragraph that establishes what the report covers and why the analysis was done, before presenting any finding.
A detailed explanation of the data sources, SQL queries, and methodology used in the analysis.
A summary of all findings, presented upfront so the reader can skip the rest of the report.
A full background section covering company history, technical definitions, and operational context.

opt_context.message: Correct. The opening section is the beginning of the narrative: a short paragraph that level-sets the reader on what the report covers and why the analysis was done, before any finding is presented.

opt_methodology.message: Detailed methodology belongs in a separate section, not the opener. The opening should be a short paragraph explaining what the publication is about — not technical definitions or data-source details.

opt_summary.message: A summary of all findings is the middle of the narrative, not the beginning. The beginning establishes context — what is happening and why — before the findings are presented.

opt_background.message: A full background section is exactly what the opening should avoid. The opening should be short and purposeful — not lengthy background before the reader knows what the report is about.

correct.message: Correct. In a story's structure, the beginning establishes context. The opening section level-sets the reader before diving into the analysis.

incorrect.message: The opening section is the beginning of the narrative — it establishes context (what the report covers and why) in a short paragraph, not methodology or lengthy background.

hints: Think about what a story's beginning does: it establishes context before the action begins.
The opening should be short and purposeful — what does the reader need to know before seeing any finding?

public.prompt: You are writing the opening context section for the QuickShip delivery report. Which sentence best fulfils the requirement to explain why the statistics were collected?

options.text: This analysis was prompted by rising customer complaints about Lagos delivery times last quarter.
Delivery times were measured using timestamps from the orders table, joined to the driver roster via courier_id.
QuickShip was founded in 2019 and has operated across Lagos, Kano, and Abuja since 2021.
Lagos average delivery time rose to 30 minutes last month, above the 25-minute target.

opt_operational.message: Correct. Explaining why the statistics were collected means including relevant, factual information about the policy and operational context — here, the rising customer complaints that prompted the review.

opt_technical.message: Technical measurement details belong in a methodology section, not the opening context. The opening should explain why the analysis was done, not how the data was extracted.

opt_history.message: Company history is background information, not the reason the statistics were collected. The opening should explain the operational or policy reason that prompted this specific analysis.

opt_finding.message: A finding belongs in the middle of the narrative, not the opening context section. The opening should explain why the analysis was done — before presenting any result.

correct.message: Correct. Explaining why the statistics were collected means including relevant, factual information about the policy and operational context — the reason the analysis exists at all.

incorrect.message: The opening context section should explain why the statistics were collected — the policy or operational reason that prompted the analysis, not technical details, history, or findings.

hints: What prompted this analysis to be done at all? That is what the opening should explain.
The opening explains why the analysis was done — not how the data was collected or what the results were.

public.instruction: Write a two-sentence opening context section for the QuickShip delivery report. The first sentence should state what the report covers and why the analysis was done. The second sentence should name the specific question the analysis answers. Do not include any findings, results, or technical methodology.
checklist: Sentence 1 states what the report covers (delivery times, cities, time period).
Sentence 1 includes the operational or policy reason the analysis was done (e.g. rising customer complaints).
Sentence 2 names the specific question the analysis answers.
Neither sentence references a finding, result, or technical detail.
The two sentences together are short — no lengthy background.

rubric.criterion: Sentence 1 states what the report covers and includes the operational reason the analysis was done.
Sentence 2 names the specific question the analysis answers.
Neither sentence references a finding, result, or technical methodology.

correct.message: Well done. Your two sentences establish what the report covers, why the analysis was done, and what question it answers — without any findings or technical background.

incorrect.message: Check your two sentences: the first should state what the report covers and why the analysis was done; the second should name the specific question it answers. Neither should include findings or technical details.

hints: Sentence 1: 'This report examines [what] across [where] [when], prompted by [why].'
Sentence 2: 'It answers: [specific question]?' — name the question, not the answer.

public.prompt: Two QuickShip checkout A/B tests both show a roughly 10% lift for the redesigned button. Test A ran with 50 users per group; Test B ran with 5,000 users per group. Which estimate is more precise, and why?

options.text: Test B (5,000 per group) — a bigger sample provides a more precise point estimate because more cases are observed.
Both are equally precise — they show the same roughly 10% lift, so the estimates are identical.
Test A (50 per group) — a smaller sample is less noisy because there are fewer data points to average.
Precision depends on the size of the lift, not the sample size.

opt_large_precise.message: Correct. A bigger sample tends to provide a more precise point estimate. With 5,000 users per group, far more completed orders are observed, so the estimate of the button's effect is more accurate.

opt_same.message: The two estimates happen to be the same number, but that does not mean they are equally precise. Precision describes how close repeated estimates would cluster around the true value — and that depends on sample size, not the observed lift.

opt_small_precise.message: A smaller sample is not less noisy — it is less precise. With only 50 users per group, the estimate could easily land far from the true value just by chance. More cases observed means a more accurate estimate.

opt_lift_matters.message: The size of the lift does not determine precision. Precision comes from how many cases are observed: a bigger sample provides a more precise point estimate regardless of the lift's magnitude.

correct.message: Right. A bigger sample provides a more precise point estimate. The 5,000-user test observed far more completed orders, so its estimate of the button's effect is more accurate.

incorrect.message: Think about what precision means: how closely repeated estimates cluster around the true value. That depends on how many cases are observed, not on the size of the lift.

hints: Which test observed more completed orders?
The more cases observed, the more accurately you can estimate the effect — regardless of what the estimate turns out to be.

public.instruction: Two QuickShip checkout A/B tests both showed a roughly 10% lift for the redesigned button. Test A ran with 50 users per group; Test B ran with 5,000 users per group. In your own words, explain which result is more trustworthy and why — referencing precision of estimation and the number of cases observed.
checklist: Identify which test is more trustworthy.
Explain that a bigger sample provides a more precise point estimate.
State that observing more cases allows a more accurate estimate of the button's effect on completed orders.

rubric.criterion: Correctly identifies the 5,000-user test as more trustworthy.
Explains that a bigger sample provides a more precise point estimate.
States that observing more cases allows a more accurate estimate of the button's effect on completed orders.

correct.message: Well done. The 5,000-user test is more trustworthy because a bigger sample provides a more precise point estimate — more cases observed means the estimate of the button's effect on completed orders is more accurate.

incorrect.message: Make sure your explanation names the 5,000-user test as more trustworthy, explains that a bigger sample is more precise, and connects that to the number of completed orders observed.

hints: Which test observed more completed orders?
Precision of estimation is the key concept — how does sample size affect it?

public.prompt: For the QuickShip checkout A/B test, which statement correctly describes the role of H0 (the null hypothesis)?

options.text: H0 represents the skeptical position — that the redesigned button makes no real difference to completion rate.
H0 represents the claim we are trying to find evidence for — that the redesigned button improves completion rate.
H0 is the observed result — the roughly 10% lift measured in the test.
H0 is the significance threshold (e.g. p < 0.05) used to decide whether to reject.

opt_skeptic.message: Correct. H0 often represents a skeptical position or a perspective of 'no difference'. For the checkout test, H0 says the button makes no real difference to completion rate.

opt_alternative.message: That describes HA (the alternative hypothesis), not H0. H0 is the skeptical position — it says nothing changed. HA is the claim under consideration that the button improves completion rate.

opt_result.message: H0 is not the observed result. It is the skeptical claim that the button makes no real difference — the baseline assumption before the test is run.

opt_threshold.message: The significance threshold (p < 0.05) is a decision rule, not H0. H0 is the skeptical claim that the button makes no real difference to completion rate.

correct.message: Right. H0 is the skeptical position — 'no difference'. HA is the alternative claim under consideration.

incorrect.message: H0 is the null hypothesis — the skeptical position that nothing changed. HA is the alternative claim you are trying to find evidence for.

hints: H0 and HA are opposites: one is skeptical, one is the claim under consideration.
Which hypothesis says the button makes no real difference?

public.prompt: The large QuickShip checkout test (5,000 per group) returns p = 0.001. What does this p-value tell you?

options.text: If H0 were true (no real difference), data at least as extreme as this would occur only 0.1% of the time — strong evidence against H0.
There is a 99.9% probability that the redesigned button genuinely improves completion rate.
The button's effect is 0.001 percentage points — a very small but real improvement.
The test has a 0.1% error rate, meaning 99.9% of the test's conclusions will be correct.

opt_correct.message: Correct. The p-value is the probability of observing data at least as favorable to HA as the current data, if H0 were true. p = 0.001 means such data would be very unusual under H0 — strong evidence against it.

opt_prob_ha.message: The p-value is not the probability that HA is true. It is the probability of observing data at least this extreme if H0 were true. A small p-value means the data would be unusual under H0, not that HA has a 99.9% chance of being correct.

opt_effect_size.message: The p-value is not the size of the effect. It is the probability of observing data at least as extreme as this if H0 were true. The effect size is the roughly 10% lift, not the p-value.

opt_error_rate.message: The p-value is not an error rate for the test's conclusions. It is the probability of observing data at least as extreme as this if H0 were true — a measure of how unusual the result would be under the null hypothesis.

correct.message: Right. The p-value quantifies how unusual the observed data would be if H0 were true. A very small p-value is strong evidence against H0.

incorrect.message: The p-value is the probability of observing data at least as extreme as this, assuming H0 is true. It is not a probability that HA is correct, not an effect size, and not an error rate.

hints: The p-value is calculated assuming H0 is true — what does it measure under that assumption?
A small p-value means the observed data would be very unusual if H0 were true.

public.intro: Use the A/B test results table to answer three questions about confidence intervals and statistical significance.

tasks.prompt: Select the variation row where the 95% confidence interval contains the null value (0% lift) — the test where we cannot reject H0.
In the large-sample test (5,000 per group) variation row, select the null_value_in_ci cell — this row shows a statistically significant result.

Select the ci_lower cell for the large-sample test (test_checkout_large) variation row. The 95% confidence interval shown there reflects the repeated-sampling behaviour of the method: if this procedure were applied to many independent samples, about 95% of the resulting intervals would contain the true parameter — not that there is a 95% probability this specific interval contains it. Identify the cell that anchors this interval.

task_ci_contains_null.correct: Correct. The small-sample test (n=50) variation row has null_value_in_ci = 'yes' — the 95% CI spans −9.4% to 29.0%, which includes 0%, so we cannot reject H0.
task_ci_contains_null.incorrect: Look for the variation row where null_value_in_ci is 'yes' — that is the test where the confidence interval contains the null value of 0% lift.

task_stat_sig_cell.correct: Correct. The large-sample test variation row shows null_value_in_ci = 'no' — the 95% CI (7.2% to 12.4%) does not include 0%, so the result is statistically significant.
task_stat_sig_cell.incorrect: Select the null_value_in_ci cell in the test_checkout_large variation row — that is the large-sample test result.

task_ci_interpretation.correct: Correct. The ci_lower value anchors the 95% confidence interval for the large-sample test. '95% confidence' describes the long-run behaviour of the method: if the sampling procedure were repeated many times, about 95% of the resulting intervals would contain the true parameter. It does not mean there is a 95% probability that this particular interval contains it.
task_ci_interpretation.incorrect: Select the ci_lower cell in the test_checkout_large variation row. That cell anchors the 95% confidence interval whose interpretation is about the long-run behaviour of the method, not a probability attached to this single interval.

correct.message: Well done. The small-sample test cannot reject H0 because 0% lift falls inside its wide CI. The large-sample test is statistically significant (CI excludes 0%). The 95% CI lower bound anchors an interval whose meaning is about the long-run behaviour of the method: about 95% of such intervals would contain the true parameter across many repeated samples — not a 95% probability attached to this one interval.

incorrect.message: Check each task: (1) find the variation row where the CI contains 0% lift; (2) find the null_value_in_ci cell for the large-sample test; (3) find the ci_lower cell for the large-sample test variation row and recall that '95% confidence' describes the long-run behaviour of the method, not a probability attached to this single interval.

hints: null_value_in_ci = 'yes' means the CI contains 0% lift — H0 cannot be rejected.

'95% confidence' means that if the procedure were repeated across many samples, about 95% of the resulting intervals would contain the true parameter — it is not a probability attached to this specific interval.

public.prompt: In the textbook proportion test, the null value is p0 = 0.333. Which statement correctly describes the role of the null value in this setup?

options.text: It is the specific value being compared to the parameter — the value H0 claims the proportion equals.
It is the proportion observed in the sample — the result the test is trying to explain.
It is the lower bound of the 95% confidence interval computed from the sample.
It is the significance level — the threshold below which we reject H0.

opt_null_value_role.message: Correct. The null value is the specific value being compared to the parameter in the hypothesis test. H0 claims the proportion equals p0 = 0.333; the test checks whether the sample data are consistent with that claim.

opt_sample_result.message: The null value is not the sample result. It is the value H0 claims the population proportion equals — the value you compare the sample against, not the value the sample produced.

opt_ci_bound.message: The null value is not a confidence interval bound. It is the specific value H0 claims the proportion equals. Whether the null value falls inside or outside the CI is what drives the reject/fail-to-reject decision.

opt_significance.message: The significance level (e.g. 0.05) is a decision threshold, not the null value. The null value is the specific proportion H0 claims — here, p0 = 0.333.

correct.message: Right. The null value is the specific value H0 claims the parameter equals. The test checks whether the sample data are consistent with that claim.

incorrect.message: The null value is the specific value H0 claims the population proportion equals — not the sample result, not a CI bound, and not the significance level.

hints: H0 makes a specific claim about the population proportion — what is that claim?
The null value is what you compare the confidence interval against to decide whether to reject H0.

public.prompt: A large online experiment finds that placing additional ads on a movie review website statistically significantly increases viewership of a TV show by 0.001%. What is the correct business conclusion?

options.text: The result is statistically significant but not practically significant — the 0.001% increase is too small to have real business value.
The result is both statistically and practically significant — statistical significance confirms the effect is real and worth acting on.
The result should be rejected — a 0.001% increase cannot be statistically significant.
No conclusion can be drawn — the sample size must have been too small to detect such a small effect.

opt_stat_not_practical.message: Correct. When the sample size is large, even a very small, practically unimportant difference can be detected and called statistically significant. A 0.001% increase in viewership is statistically significant but has no practical value.

opt_both_sig.message: Statistical significance does not imply practical importance. With a large enough sample, even a trivially small effect can be statistically significant. A 0.001% increase in viewership is not worth acting on, even if the p-value is very small.

opt_reject_result.message: A 0.001% increase can be statistically significant when the sample is very large — that is precisely the point. Large samples can detect even tiny differences. The issue is whether the detected difference has practical value.

opt_need_more.message: The scenario states the result is statistically significant, which means the sample was large enough to detect the effect. The issue is not sample size — it is that the detected effect (0.001%) has no practical value.

correct.message: Right. Large samples can make even trivially small differences statistically significant. Statistical significance tells you the effect is unlikely to be zero — it does not tell you the effect is large enough to matter.

incorrect.message: Statistical significance and practical importance are different. A large sample can detect a 0.001% difference as statistically significant — but that does not mean the difference has any practical value.

hints: What happens to the ability to detect small effects when the sample size is very large?
Statistical significance tells you the effect is unlikely to be zero — not that it is large enough to matter.

public.prompt: An A/B test summary card shows: control conversion rate = 0.82, treatment conversion rate = 0.90, 95% CI for the lift = [−9.4%, 29.0%], null value = 0% lift. Arrange the four reasoning steps in the correct order to reach a business conclusion.

items.text: Locate the null value (0% lift) relative to the confidence interval: 0% falls inside [−9.4%, 29.0%].
State the reject/fail-to-reject decision: the null value is inside the CI, so we fail to reject H0.
Correct the fail-to-reject misconception: failing to reject H0 does not mean H0 is true — the sample of 50 may simply be too small to detect a real difference.
Write the business conclusion: there is not sufficient evidence that the redesigned button changes completion rate — but this may reflect limited sample size, not absence of an effect.

follow_up.prompt: Which step is most often skipped, leading analysts to incorrectly conclude the button has no effect?

options.text: Step 3 — correcting the fail-to-reject misconception.
Step 1 — locating the null value relative to the CI.
Step 2 — stating the reject/fail-to-reject decision.

grading.loop_back_note: The null value must be located first (step 1), then the decision stated (step 2), then the misconception corrected (step 3), then the business conclusion written (step 4). Skipping step 3 leads to the error of treating 'fail to reject' as 'null is true'.

correct.message: Well done. The correct sequence: locate the null value in the CI → state the decision → correct the misconception (fail to reject ≠ null is true) → write the business conclusion. The small sample may simply be too small to detect a real difference.

incorrect.message: The four steps must follow this logic: first locate the null value relative to the CI, then state the decision, then correct the fail-to-reject misconception, then write the business conclusion.

hints: Start by checking whether the null value (0% lift) falls inside or outside the confidence interval.
Failing to reject H0 is not the same as concluding H0 is true — the sample may just be too small.

public.prompt: The QuickShip operations team says: 'Deliveries feel slow lately — can you look into it?' Which of the following is a correctly scoped business question?

options.text: Which delivery zones are missing the 25-minute target, and by how much, over the last quarter?
Why are deliveries slow?
What is happening with QuickShip's operations?
Should QuickShip hire more couriers?

opt_scoped.message: Correct. This question names the context (last quarter's orders), the measure (delivery time vs. the 25-minute target), and the unit of comparison (delivery zones) — all three elements of a properly scoped business question.

opt_vague.message: This is still vague — it does not identify the context (which orders, which time period), the measure (delivery time vs. what target?), or the unit of comparison (which zones or cities?). Scoping requires all three.

opt_too_broad.message: This is too broad to be analytical. A scoped business question must identify the context, the measure, and the unit of comparison — not just name the company and a vague area of concern.

opt_solution.message: This jumps to a solution before the analysis is done. A scoped business question identifies what the analysis will measure and compare — it does not pre-suppose the answer.

correct.message: Right. A scoped business question identifies the context, the measure, and the unit of comparison — so the analyst and the stakeholder share the same understanding of what the analysis will and will not answer.

incorrect.message: A scoped business question must name: (1) the context (which data, which time period), (2) the measure (what is being compared), and (3) the unit of comparison (zones, cities, etc.).

hints: Does the question name a specific time period and dataset?
Does the question name a specific measure (e.g. delivery time vs. a target) and a unit of comparison (e.g. zones)?

public.instruction: Write a one-sentence business question for a capstone dataset of your choice. Your question must identify: (1) the context — what data and what time period or scope; (2) the boundaries — what measure and unit of comparison the analysis will address. Use the QuickShip example as a model: 'Which delivery zones are missing the 25-minute target, and by how much, over the last quarter?'
checklist: The question names a specific dataset or data source.
The question names a specific time period or scope.
The question names a specific measure (what is being compared or evaluated).
The question names a unit of comparison (e.g. zones, cities, products).
The question makes clear what the analysis will and will not answer.

rubric.criterion: Names a specific measurable question with context and boundaries.
States the context (what data, what time period or scope).
States the boundaries (what measure and unit of comparison).
Makes clear what the analysis will and will not answer.

correct.message: Well done. Your scoped question names the context and boundaries, so the analyst and stakeholder share the same understanding of what the analysis will and will not answer.

incorrect.message: Check your question against the checklist: does it name the data, the time period, the measure, and the unit of comparison? A vague question cannot guide the rest of the analysis.

hints: Start with: 'Which [unit of comparison] are [measure] [condition], over [time period]?'
The QuickShip example names zones, delivery time vs. target, and last quarter — use that as a template.

options.text: A: SQL query via pandas.io.sql; B: read_excel().
A: SQL query via pandas.io.sql; B: SQL query via pandas.io.sql.
A: read_excel(); B: read_excel().
A: read_excel(); B: SQL query via pandas.io.sql.

opt_correct.message: Correct. Data in a SQL database is retrieved with a SQL query via pandas.io.sql. An Excel workbook is read directly into a DataFrame with read_excel(). The retrieval method follows the source.

opt_both_sql.message: SQL queries work for SQL databases, but not for Excel workbooks. An Excel workbook is read with read_excel(), not a SQL query.

opt_both_excel.message: read_excel() reads Excel files, not SQL databases. Data in a SQL database is retrieved with a SQL query via pandas.io.sql.

opt_swapped.message: The methods are swapped. read_excel() reads Excel files; SQL queries via pandas.io.sql retrieve data from SQL databases. The retrieval method must match where the data lives.

correct.message: Right. The retrieval method follows the source: SQL query for the database, read_excel() for the workbook.

incorrect.message: Match the retrieval method to where the data lives: SQL databases use SQL queries via pandas.io.sql; Excel workbooks use read_excel().

hints: Where does each data source live — in a database or in a file?
pandas.io.sql is for SQL databases; read_excel() is for Excel files.

public.prompt: Classify each data source by the correct retrieval method. Drag each item into the 'SQL query via pandas.io.sql' bucket or the 'read_excel()' bucket.

items.text: QuickShip orders table — stored in a relational SQL database
Monthly sales records — stored in a company SQL database
Customer survey responses — exported as survey_results.xlsx

role_map.bucket_sql: SQL database sources — retrieved with a SQL query via pandas.io.sql
role_map.bucket_excel: Excel workbook sources — read directly with read_excel()

item_orders_db.message: Correct. The orders table lives in a SQL database, so it is retrieved with a SQL query via pandas.io.sql.

item_driver_xlsx.message: Correct. The driver roster is an Excel workbook (.xlsx), so it is read with read_excel().

item_sales_db.message: Correct. Monthly sales records in a SQL database are retrieved with a SQL query via pandas.io.sql.

item_survey_xlsx.message: Correct. A .xlsx file is an Excel workbook, so it is read with read_excel().

correct.message: Well done. SQL databases → SQL query via pandas.io.sql; Excel workbooks (.xlsx) → read_excel(). The retrieval method follows where the data lives.

incorrect.message: Match the retrieval method to where the data lives. SQL databases use SQL queries via pandas.io.sql. Excel workbooks (.xlsx) use read_excel().

hints: Look at the file extension or storage type: .xlsx = Excel workbook; SQL database = SQL query.
The retrieval method must match where the data lives — database or file.

public.prompt: Which of the following correctly describes the order of the first three stages in the QuickShip capstone workflow?

options.text: Scope → Retrieve → Clean/Model
Retrieve → Scope → Clean/Model
Scope → Analyze → Retrieve
Clean/Model → Scope → Retrieve

opt_correct.message: Correct. The workflow begins with scoping the question, then retrieving the source data, then cleaning and modeling it. Quality is assessed at every stage, with cleaning focused as early as possible.

opt_retrieve_first.message: Retrieving data before scoping the question means you do not yet know what data you need. Scoping comes first — it defines the question, context, and boundaries that guide every later stage.

opt_analyze_early.message: You cannot analyze data before retrieving it. The correct order is Scope → Retrieve → Clean/Model → Analyze. Scoping defines the question; retrieval brings in the data; cleaning prepares it for analysis.

opt_clean_first.message: You cannot clean data before scoping the question or retrieving the data. The workflow must start with scoping, then retrieval, then cleaning.

correct.message: Right. Scope → Retrieve → Clean/Model are the first three stages. Scoping defines the question; retrieval brings in the data; cleaning prepares it for analysis.

incorrect.message: The workflow must start with scoping the question — you cannot retrieve or clean data before you know what question you are answering.

hints: Which stage defines the question, context, and boundaries that guide everything else?
You cannot retrieve data before you know what question you are answering.

public.prompt: During the cleaning stage, you discover that 'last quarter' is ambiguous in the orders database — it could mean the calendar quarter or the fiscal quarter. What should you do?

options.text: Revisit the scoping stage to clarify the time-period boundary with the operations team before continuing.
Pick one interpretation and proceed — the analysis will be the same either way.
Skip the ambiguous rows and continue with the data that is clearly within the quarter.
Run the analysis twice — once for each interpretation — and present both results.

opt_revisit_scope.message: Correct. A phase such as scoping may need to be revisited if a later phase encounters changes or limitations. An ambiguous time-period boundary is a scoping issue — it must be resolved with the stakeholder before the analysis can proceed correctly.

opt_pick_one.message: Picking an interpretation without checking with the stakeholder risks answering the wrong question. The scoping stage established the boundaries of the analysis — an ambiguity there must be resolved by revisiting scoping.

opt_skip.message: Skipping ambiguous rows changes the scope of the analysis without the stakeholder's knowledge. The correct action is to revisit the scoping stage and clarify the boundary with the operations team.

opt_both.message: Running the analysis twice without resolving the ambiguity leaves the stakeholder to choose between two results they did not ask for. The correct action is to revisit scoping and agree on the correct time-period boundary.

correct.message: Right. A later phase discovering an ambiguity in the original question is exactly when scoping must be revisited. The workflow is not strictly linear — earlier phases can be returned to when needed.

incorrect.message: An ambiguity in the time-period boundary is a scoping issue. The correct action is to revisit the scoping stage and clarify with the stakeholder — not to pick an interpretation unilaterally.

hints: Which stage established the time-period boundary for the analysis?
The workflow allows earlier phases to be revisited when a later phase encounters a limitation.

public.prompt: Put the six QuickShip capstone workflow stages in the correct order. Then use the follow-up question to identify which stage connects the orders and drivers tables.

items.text: Scope — define the business question, context, and boundaries
Retrieve — pull the orders table via SQL query and the driver roster via read_excel()
Clean/Model — handle missing values, assess data quality, and connect the orders and drivers tables
Visualize — build charts and summary tables
Communicate — deliver findings to the operations team

follow_up.prompt: Which stage connects the orders and drivers tables using driver_id as the join key?

options.text: Clean/Model — the modeling stage connects related tables.
Retrieve — the retrieval stage joins tables when pulling data.
Analyze — the analysis stage merges tables as needed.

grading.loop_back_note: Scope must come first. Retrieve follows. Clean/Model is where multi-table relationships are connected (modeling). Analyze, Visualize, and Communicate complete the workflow. Quality is assessed at every stage.

correct.message: Well done. The correct order is Scope → Retrieve → Clean/Model → Analyze → Visualize → Communicate. The Clean/Model stage is where the orders and drivers tables are connected using driver_id as the join key.

incorrect.message: The workflow must start with Scope (define the question), then Retrieve (pull the data), then Clean/Model (handle quality and connect tables), then Analyze, Visualize, and Communicate.

hints: Scoping always comes first — you cannot retrieve data before you know what question you are answering.
The modeling stage is where multi-table relationships are connected — which stage is that?

public.prompt: During the analysis phase of the QuickShip capstone, you discover that one delivery zone has far fewer orders than expected. What should you do?

options.text: Record the discovery in your decision log, note how you handled it, and continue — monitoring whether it affects the analysis's relevance to the original question.
Ignore it and proceed — minor data issues do not affect the overall conclusion.
Restart the analysis from scratch — the plan is no longer valid.
Report the issue to the operations team immediately and wait for their instructions before continuing.

opt_record_monitor.message: Correct. During the analysis phase, appropriate records of the analysis conducted, changes, decisions, and assumptions made are maintained, while progress and relevance are monitored. Recording the discovery and how you handled it is exactly what the decision log is for.

opt_ignore.message: Ignoring a data issue without recording it violates the requirement to maintain appropriate records of changes and decisions. Even minor issues should be logged so the analysis remains transparent.

opt_restart.message: Restarting from scratch is not necessary for every data issue. The analysis phase involves monitoring progress and relevance and recording decisions — not abandoning the plan at the first complication.

opt_report_only.message: Stopping to wait for instructions is not always necessary. The analysis phase involves carrying out the planned analysis while monitoring and recording decisions. Record the issue and continue, flagging it in the decision log for the stakeholder's awareness.

correct.message: Right. The analysis phase requires maintaining records of changes, decisions, and assumptions while monitoring whether the analysis still answers the original question. That is what the decision log is for.

incorrect.message: During the analysis phase, you carry out the planned analysis while monitoring progress and relevance, and maintaining records of changes, decisions, and assumptions. Record the issue and continue.

hints: What is the purpose of a decision log during the analysis phase?
The analysis phase involves monitoring and recording — not ignoring issues or restarting.

public.instruction: Complete the QuickShip capstone project's execution independently against its plan, across the SQL, spreadsheet, and Python/pandas tools it requires. Maintain a decision log throughout. Submit your completed capstone artefact (queries, cleaned data, model, statistics, and figures) together with a short decision log.
checklist: Completed SQL query retrieving the orders table.
Completed read_excel() import of the driver roster.
Cleaned data with missing values handled.
Joined orders and drivers tables using driver_id.
Zone-level delivery statistics computed.
At least one visualization produced.
Decision log records changes made to the original plan, how data-quality issues were handled, and a check that outputs still answer the original question.

rubric.criterion: Submits a completed capstone artefact (queries, cleaned data, model, statistics, and figures).
Decision log records changes made to the original plan.
Decision log records how data-quality issues were handled.
Decision log includes a check that outputs still answer the original analytical question.

correct.message: Well done. You completed the capstone independently and maintained a decision log that records changes, data-quality decisions, and a check that the outputs still answer the original question.

incorrect.message: Make sure your submission includes both the completed artefact and a decision log. The log must record changes to the plan, how data-quality issues were handled, and a check that the outputs still answer the original question.

hints: The decision log is not optional — it is what makes the analysis transparent and evaluable.
Check that your outputs answer the original scoped question: which zones miss the 25-minute target, and by how much?

public.prompt: The Head of Operations receives the QuickShip capstone summary pack. What is the standard for whether the delivery is sufficient?

options.text: The summary pack lets the Head of Operations determine whether the work meets their requirements — whether it answers the original question.
The summary pack is at least five pages long and includes all the raw data.
The summary pack includes all the technical details of the SQL queries and Python code used.
The summary pack has been approved by the data team before being sent to the operations team.

opt_sufficient.message: Correct. During delivery, insights are communicated to the people who need them, sufficiently for them to determine whether the work meets their requirements. The standard is whether the Head of Operations can judge whether the analysis answers the original question.

opt_length.message: Length and inclusion of raw data are not the standard for sufficiency. The standard is whether the recipient can determine whether the work meets their requirements — whether it answers the original question.

opt_technical.message: Technical details of the implementation are not the standard for sufficiency. The standard is whether the Head of Operations can determine whether the analysis answers the original question — not whether they can reproduce the SQL queries.

opt_approval.message: Internal approval is not the standard for sufficiency. The standard is whether the recipient — the Head of Operations — can determine whether the work meets their requirements.

correct.message: Right. Delivery is sufficient when the recipient can determine whether the work meets their requirements. For the capstone, that means the Head of Operations can judge whether the analysis answers the original question.

incorrect.message: The standard for sufficiency is not length, technical detail, or internal approval. It is whether the recipient can determine whether the work meets their requirements.

hints: Who is the audience for the delivery, and what do they need to be able to do with it?
Sufficiency is about the recipient's ability to evaluate the work — not about the format or length.

public.instruction: Using the QuickShip zone delivery summary, write a narrated stakeholder summary addressed to the Head of Operations. Structure it with a clear beginning (business context and the 25-minute delivery target), middle (the zone-delay finding with key numbers), and end (a recommended next step). Frame the finding in terms that motivate the Head of Operations. Submit your summary pack.
checklist: Beginning: states the business context and the 25-minute delivery target.
Middle: names the specific zones missing the target and by how much (e.g. Lagos-North: avg 32.9 min, gap 7.9 min).
End: gives a recommended next step.
Addressed to the Head of Operations — framed around what they care about.
No unexplained technical detail (no SQL, no Python code).

rubric.criterion: Has a clear beginning that states the business context and the 25-minute delivery target.
Middle presents the specific zone-delay finding with numbers (zones and gap in minutes).
End gives a recommended next step.
Addressed to a named audience role and framed in terms that audience cares about.
Does not include unexplained technical detail.

correct.message: Well done. Your summary has a clear beginning (context and target), middle (specific zone findings with numbers), and end (recommended next step), framed for the Head of Operations.

incorrect.message: Check your summary against the checklist: does it have a beginning (context and target), a middle (specific zones and gap numbers), and an end (recommended next step)? Is it framed for the Head of Operations without unexplained technical detail?

hints: The beginning should answer: what is this report about, and why does it matter to the Head of Operations?
The middle should name specific zones and their gap above the 25-minute target — use the numbers from the zone summary.

public.prompt: Which of the following is a valid delivery and communication activity for the QuickShip capstone?

options.text: Producing a summary pack and presenting it to the operations team that raised the original complaint.
Sending the raw orders table and driver roster to the operations team for them to analyze themselves.
Sharing the Python notebook with the SQL queries and pandas code, without any narrative.
Filing the analysis in an internal data team repository without communicating it to the operations team.

opt_summary_pack.message: Correct. Delivery and communication activities can include producing summary packs and reports, launching dashboards or websites, and giving presentations. The capstone's deliverable is the finished report or summary pack, presented to the operations team that raised the original complaint.

opt_raw_data.message: Sending raw data is not a delivery activity — it transfers the analytical work to the stakeholder rather than communicating insights. Delivery means communicating the insights to the people who need them.

opt_code_only.message: Sharing code without a narrative does not communicate insights to a non-technical audience. Delivery activities include summary packs, reports, and presentations — not raw code.

opt_internal_only.message: Filing the analysis internally without communicating it to the operations team means the insights never reach the people who need them. Delivery means communicating to the commissioner and approver.

correct.message: Right. Delivery activities include summary packs, reports, dashboards, and presentations — communicated to the people who need the insights.

incorrect.message: Delivery means communicating insights to the people who need them. Valid formats include summary packs, reports, dashboards, and presentations — not raw data, code, or internal filing.

hints: Who is the audience for the capstone delivery?
Delivery activities communicate insights — they do not transfer raw data or code.

public.instruction: Write up and present the finished QuickShip capstone project as a polished deliverable. Produce a documentation section that records the key analytical decisions, assumptions, data-handling choices, and quality-assurance checks made at each stage. Then assemble the finished report or summary pack together with the visualization set and present it to the operations team.
checklist: Documentation section records at least three analytical decisions or assumptions (e.g. how missing values were handled, how the time period was defined, how the join key was verified).
Documentation covers decisions at multiple stages (e.g. scoping, cleaning, modeling).
Completed summary pack or report paired with the visualization set.
Plain-language narrative addressed to the stakeholder who raised the original question.
No unexplained technical jargon in the stakeholder-facing narrative.

rubric.criterion: Documentation section explicitly records at least three analytical decisions or assumptions.
Documentation covers decisions at multiple stages of the workflow.
Completed summary pack or report paired with the visualization set.
Plain-language narrative addressed to the stakeholder who raised the original question.

correct.message: Well done. Your deliverable includes a documentation section with explicit analytical decisions and a completed summary pack with visualizations, addressed to the operations team.

incorrect.message: Check your submission against the checklist: does the documentation section record at least three analytical decisions? Does the summary pack include visualizations and a plain-language narrative for the operations team?

hints: The documentation section should record decisions at each stage — scoping, cleaning, modeling, analysis.
The summary pack is for the operations team — it should be in plain language, not technical jargon.
